Q: AttributeError: module 'aiobotocore' has no attribute 'AioSession' when reading csv from s3_path using Pandas A:

This is very likely caused by versions that do not meat requirements (either pandas or other). As you can see the AttributeError is raised from s3fs package. I've just encountered similar issue and the problem was mismatch in the requirements. I would recommend to check the following packages:

  • pandas

  • s3fs

  • fsspec

  • aibotocore

And if compatible requirements are installed (e.g. in my case it was outdated s3fs package). I would recommend to install all the required dependencies in a fresh virtual env.

See also this thread.

Q: How to urlencode data for curl command? A:

The question is about doing this in bash and there's no need for python or perl as there is in fact a single command that does exactly what you want - "urlencode" (https://www.gridsite.org/doc/HEAD/urlencode.1.html).

value=$(urlencode "${2}")

This is also much better, as the above perl answer, for example, doesn't encode all characters correctly. Try it with the long dash you get from Word and you get the wrong encoding.

Note, you need "gridsite-clients" installed to provide this command:

sudo apt install gridsite-clients

Q: Java: How to compare two Times/Dates A:

tl;dr

LocalDateTime
.parse( 
    "2011-9-5 0:00" ,
    DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "uuuu-M-d H:mm" )  // Define formatting pattern to match non-standard input.
)
.isBefore( otherLocalDateTime )

Avoid legacy date-time classes

Never use the terribly-flawed legacy classes such as Date, Calendar, SimpleDateFormat, etc.

Use only the modern java.time classes built into Java 8 and later.

ISO 8601

Ideally you would educate the publisher of your data about using only the standard date-time formats defined in ISO 8601. The standard uses leading padding zeroes. So standard inputs would be:

2011-09-05
00:00

The java.time classes use the standard formats by default when generating/parsing text. So no need to specify a formatting pattern for standard inputs.

LocalDate.parse( "2011-09-05" )
LocalTime.parse( "00:00" )

DateTimeFormatter

Your inputs are non-standard. So we must define formatting pattern to match your custom or localized formats.

DateTimeFormatter dateFormatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "uuuu-M-d" );
LocalDate date = LocalDate.parse( "2011-9-5" , dateFormatter );

DateTimeFormatter timeFormatter = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern( "H:mm" );
LocalTime time = LocalTime.parse( "0:00" , timeFormatter );

See this code run at Ideone.com.

In real work, you might cache the DateTimeFormatter objects as static final. The java.time classes are thread-safe, so you need only a singleton.

LocalDateTime

You can combine the date with the time-of-day into a LocalDateTime object.

LocalDateTime ldt = LocalDateTime.of( date , time ) ;

How can i compare this value as a Time with some other Time

Use the comparison methods isEqual, isBefore, and isAfter.

boolean earlier = ldt.isBefore( other ) ;

Time zone

Be aware: A date with time is inherently ambiguous, insufficient to determine a point on the timeline.

To determine a moment, a point on the timeline, you need the context of a time zone. For example, was your input of midnight meant to be midnight in Tokyo Japan, midnight in Toulouse France, or midnight in Toledo Ohio US — three different moments, several hours apart? Without a time zone, we have no way to know.

To determine a moment, apply a time zone or an offset-from-UTC.

ZoneId zone = ZoneId.of( "America/Edmonton" ); 
ZonedDateTime zdt = ldt.atZone( zone ) ;  // Determining a point on the timeline.

I think the problem is in my Android Studio emulator (the comment above from Tim Katzgrau). Q: Is there an easy way to reverse the ordering of a scale inside an aes() inside a geom()? A:

(This is a very old question, but I had the same issue and couldn't find an answer. The previous solution by @hugh-allan is, as indicated in the Edit note, producing an incorrect legend.)

The settings of the scale should really be in the scale_alpha* parameter. That's where you manage this. The geoms are used for adding the data or setting a style for all points, not tuning a specific scale (otherwise, it would need to be inside the aes() mapping).

The solution is to use transform = "reverse" (as of 2026, ggplot v4.0.1):

tibble(x = 1:10, y = 1) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x, y, alpha = x)) +
  geom_point(size = 5) +
  scale_alpha_continuous(transform = "reverse")

(Edit, 2026-02-13: Updated to use transform = "reverse" to match the current ggplot functionality, as suggested by aurelien in the comments.)
